title: Manyur akārṣīt: “anger did it”
theme: An offering formula in which the speaker attributes past wrongs to anger, not to himself, and offers ghee to anger as a deity; its pair, 10.61, does the same with desire.

words.context: anon: «मन्युः कोपाभिमानी देव» — the deity who presides over anger
anon: «मन्यवे क्रोधरूपाय» — whose form is anger

sandhi.type: -uḥ before a vowel; t before a nasal
sandhi.rule: manyuḥ + akārṣīt → manyur akārṣīt: after a vowel other than a/ā the visarga becomes r before a voiced sound; akārṣīt + manyuḥ → akārṣīn manyuḥ: t becomes n before m.
akārṣīt + namaḥ → akārṣīn namaḥ: t becomes n before n.

sandhi.type: unjoined vowels; eṣaḥ before a consonant
sandhi.rule: kārayitā eṣaḥ is printed without joining the vowels (see sandhi_exceptions); eṣaḥ + te → eṣa te: eṣaḥ drops its visarga before a consonant.

sandhi_exceptions.note: kārayitā eṣa is printed with the vowels apart, at the break between the confession and the offering formula.

morphology.note: s-aorist 3rd singular of √kṛ: ‘has done’ — the deed is past and complete.
Agent noun in -tṛ: ‘the doer’, set against kārayitā, the causative agent noun ‘the one who has [it] done’.
Agent noun from the causative kāraya-: ‘the one who causes [another] to act’.

translation.literal: Anger has done [it]; homage, homage. Anger has done [it]; anger does [it], I do not do [it]; anger is the doer, I am not the doer; anger is the one who causes [it] to be done, I am not the one who causes [it] to be done. This [offering] is for you, O Anger, for anger. Svāhā.
translation.readable: Anger did it — homage, homage. Anger did it: anger acts, not I; anger is the doer, not I; anger drives the deed, not I. This offering is yours, Anger: to Anger, svāhā.

syntax: A short salutation, then three parallel pairs of clauses, each setting anger against ‘I’ with the negation na: anger does / I do not; anger is the doer / I am not; anger has it done / I do not. The last sentence is an offering formula: eṣa te … svāhā, ‘this is for you’, with the vocative and the dative of the deity.

ambiguities.note: The text names no deed; as with 10.61, the anonymous commentator takes it as the sins already spoken of («अन्यत्पूर्ववत्» — the rest as before).

Read literally, the speaker says he is not the doer. The commentator discusses this directly (see commentary): the guilt lies with the one who compels, not with an unwilling doer, and the formula is spoken in remorse.

metre.name: prose
metre.note: A prose formula (yajus). The salutation counts 9 syllables, the rest 45.

beginner: This is a short offering formula. The speaker says that anger did the wrong — not he himself. Anger acted, anger was the doer, anger made him do it; then he offers a spoonful of ghee into the fire to Anger, honoured as a deity, with the word svāhā. The previous anuvāka has the same words for desire. The old commentator does not read this as an excuse. He says it is spoken by someone in remorse, who feels pushed by desire and anger into acts he did not want, and asks the deity to take the wrong away. The edition reports that reading and makes no claim about what the rite achieves.
analogy: Like someone who, looking back on an outburst, says “that was my temper talking”, and wants to be rid of the temper rather than to escape the blame.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: It salutes, then three times sets anger against ‘I’: anger does, is the doer, has [it] done; I do not, am not, have not. It ends by offering ‘this’ to Anger with svāhā.

commentary.q: How does the commentator gloss anger?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: He makes Manyu the deity who presides over anger, «मन्युः कोपाभिमानी देव», and the dative ‘to Manyu’ as ‘whose form is anger’, «मन्यवे क्रोधरूपाय»; the rest is as in the formula on desire: «अन्यत्पूर्ववत्».

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: He raises the question as a point of mīmāṃsā: «कारयितुरेव पापं न कर्तुरनिच्छतः» — the sin belongs to the one who makes another act, not to the unwilling doer; but «यदि स्वयमपीच्छत्यन्योऽपि कारयति तर्ह्युभयोरपि पापलेपः» — if the doer also wants it, both are stained. To the objection that the dharmaśāstras prescribe expiation even for sins done under compulsion, «ननु बलात्कारितपापस्यापि धर्मशास्त्रेषु प्रायश्चित्तं श्रूयत इति चेन्न», he answers that such sins are lighter. He pictures the speaker lifting his hands and weeping: «काममन्यू बलात्पापं मां कारयतोऽनिच्छन्तमपि किं करोमि क्व गच्छामि» — desire and anger force sin on me against my will; what can I do, where can I go? — and concludes «तस्माद्रोदनपश्चातापादिवशादेवमवगम्यते कारयितुरेव पापं न कर्तुरिति».

schools.disagreement: No Vedānta school commentary on this formula is in the edition’s sources: the anonymous bhāṣya reads it as a ritual formula of remorse, and neither Sāyaṇa nor Bhāskara comments on it in the copies used (their 64-anuvāka texts do not include it). Raṅgarāmānuja’s commentary is not in the sources. No school position is given.

parallels.quote: अथ केन प्रयुक्तोऽयं पापं चरति पूरुषः
parallels.note: Arjuna asks what drives a person to wrong ‘even unwilling, as if by force’ — the situation the anonymous commentator describes for this formula.
The Gītā’s answer names the same two forces as the paired formulas 10.61–10.62: desire and anger.

contemporary.text: The formula separates the self from an impulse it does not endorse: “anger did it, not I.” Read with the commentator, it is not an alibi but a way of naming the impulse so that it can be given up. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: When anger pushes you into something, do you experience it as “me” or as something acting on you?
reflect.deeper: The commentator says the guilt lies with the one who compels, not the unwilling doer, yet the speaker still makes an offering. What does that combination say about responsibility?
reflect.practice: Next time anger rises, name it silently (“this is anger”) before you act.

references.text: Only the anonymous bhāṣya of the Ānandāśrama pariśiṣṭa comments on this anuvāka in the edition’s sources; no comment is found in Sāyaṇa’s or Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara’s copies.

flags.note: Whether the formula disclaims responsibility is a question of reading; the commentator’s view (guilt lies with the compeller; the formula is spoken in remorse) is reported, not adopted.
The commentator’s example of a compelling agent («यथा कश्चिद्यवनोऽनिच्छन्तमपि कंचित्पापमकारयत्») is his own; the edition reports his argument and does not adopt its example.
